stages.title: Henry VIII & The Birth of King-in-Parliament
stages.trigger: Henry VIII severed the English Church from Rome by using parliamentary statutes, inadvertently elevating Parliament into a supreme legislative partner.
stages.connective: Created the enduring constitutional doctrine of the ‘King-in-Parliament’, ensuring all future royal religious changes required parliamentary consent.
stages.question: How did Henry VIII’s Break with Rome strengthen Parliament’s role?

stages.title: Elizabethan Compromise & Patriotic Solidarity
stages.trigger: Elizabeth I worked cooperatively with Parliament to preserve the Middle Way against Catholic assassination conspiracies and the Spanish Armada.
stages.connective: Fused Protestant religious identity with English national sovereignty, creating a shared constitutional bond between Crown and elected MPs.
stages.question: How did Elizabeth’s settlement and the Armada unite Protestant England?

stages.title: Stuart Absolutism & The Divine Right Collision
stages.actor: James I, Charles I & Dissident MPs
stages.trigger: Stuart monarchs asserted absolute Divine Right authority, ruling without Parliament and extracting arbitrary taxes like Ship Money without voter consent.
stages.connective: Radically alienated the landed gentry and urban merchants, turning constitutional debates over taxation into an ideological struggle over sovereignty.
stages.question: Why did Stuart Divine Right claims cause a clash with MPs by 1640?

stages.title: Civil War Cataclysm & Judicial Regicide
stages.actor: New Model Army & The Rump Parliament
stages.trigger: Parliament’s citizen army defeated the Royalists in the Civil War, trying and beheading Charles I as a traitor who waged war against his own realm.
stages.connective: Proved that sovereign power derived from the people rather than heavenly appointment, permanently destroying the inviolability of kings.
stages.question: Why was the 1649 execution of Charles I a turning point for monarchy?

stages.title: The Bill of Rights & Parliamentary Supremacy
stages.trigger: The 1689 Bill of Rights formally made the Crown subject to the rule of law, stripping kings of the power to raise money or suspend statutes without MPs.
stages.connective: Concluded the 170-year struggle by firmly enthroning Parliamentary Supremacy and establishing the foundation of Britain’s modern democracy.
stages.question: How did the 1689 Bill of Rights shift power from Crown to Parliament?

lessons.did_you_know: Between 1517 and 1689, the constitutional structure of Britain completely flipped upside down! In 1517, King Henry answered to the Pope in Rome, and ordinary peasants had to pay church tithes under threat of eternal damnation. By 1689, King William answered to an elected Parliament of landowners, the Pope was barred by law from ever touching English soil, and no monarch could levy a single penny of tax without parliamentary consent!

items.question: What belief held that kings were appointed directly by God and could not be questioned by Parliament?
items.explanation: Divine Right asserted that monarchs answered only to God Almighty, not to earthly laws or courts.

items.question: Where did King Charles I raise his Royal Standard in August 1642, officially beginning the Civil War?
items.explanation: Charles fled London and raised the Royal Standard at Nottingham.

items.question: In what year did Oliver Cromwell form the disciplined, merit-based New Model Army?
items.explanation: The New Model Army was established in 1645, winning a decisive victory at the Battle of Naseby.

items.question: On what exact date was King Charles I publicly beheaded outside Whitehall Banqueting House?
items.explanation: Charles I was executed on 30 January 1649, wearing two shirts against the freezing weather.

items.question: Which Protestant leader was invited by seven leading nobles in 1688 to invade England in the Glorious Revolution?
items.explanation: In 1688, seven leading nobles invited Protestant William of Orange and his wife Mary to invade England.

items.question: What ancient coastal tax did Charles I illegally force inland towns to pay during his Personal Rule?
items.explanation: Ship Money was traditionally paid by ports in wartime; Charles forced inland counties to pay it in peacetime.

items.question: Rebellion in which kingdom forced King Charles I to end his Personal Rule and recall Parliament in 1640?
items.explanation: When Scots rebelled against Charles's religious policies, military bankruptcy forced the King to summon Parliament in 1640.

items.question: What decisive 1645 battle proved the military superiority of the New Model Army over Royalist forces?
items.explanation: At the Battle of Naseby in June 1645, the disciplined Parliamentary cavalry smashed the King’s army.

items.question: What event in December 1648 saw Colonel Pride arrest moderate MPs, leaving the "Rump Parliament"?
items.explanation: Pride’s Purge removed MPs who wished to negotiate with the King, clearing the path for his trial.

items.question: What was the return of the monarchy in 1660 under Charles II officially called?
items.explanation: Following eleven years of Puritan rule, the monarchy was brought back in the 1660 Restoration.

lessons.prologue: Over two turbulent centuries, England was transformed by religious reformation, naval war, bloody regicide, and political revolution. Through every clash, one fundamental question tested the kingdom: where does supreme authority truly lie? In 1689, the Bill of Rights stripped monarchs of absolute power forever. Which turning point between 1517 and 1689 mattered most?

narrative_blocks.title: Henry VIII & Sovereign Statehood (1517–1547)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] The Break with Rome transformed national authority. Under Henry VIII, the Pope lost all English power as the Crown established sovereign national independence. Crucially, Henry achieved this not by royal decree, but through statute law passed by the Reformation Parliament.

New laws made with MPs forged an unprecedented partnership between King and Parliament. Furthermore, vast monastery lands given away or sold to local gentry bound England’s landowning classes to royal supremacy, laying the foundations of modern English parliamentary sovereignty.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: The Great Seal of England showing the Commons in session and the sovereign state authority
narrative_blocks.caption: The Great Seal of England, representing sovereign constitutional authority and the transition from royal prerogative to parliamentary statute (The National Archives, PRO 30/26/1).

source.title: Source A (Royal Sovereignty): The Act of Supremacy 1534 (26 Hen. 8 c. 1)
source.caption: The foundation statute of the English Reformation declaring King Henry VIII to be the sole supreme head on earth of the Church of England.
source.author: Reformation Parliament of England under King Henry VIII
source.content: Albeit the King’s Majesty justly and rightfully is and oweth to be the supreme head of the Church of England... Be it enacted by authority of this present Parliament, that the King our sovereign lord, his heirs and successors kings of this realm, shall be taken, accepted, and reputed the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England called Anglicana Ecclesia.
source.question: How did Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy in 1534 lay the groundwork for 150 years of religious and political turmoil in England?
source.model_answer: By uniting spiritual and temporal sword in the Crown, Henry abolished papal authority and made religious doctrine a matter of royal command. Every subsequent monarch could reshape church law, turning succession into a life-or-death ideological battleground between Catholics, Anglicans, and Puritans.
source.context: In 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, officially severing England from the Roman Catholic Church and vesting supreme ecclesiastical power in the monarch.
source.hinge_question: Looking back across 1517–1689, was Henry VIII the creator of royal power or the accidental spark of its ultimate downfall?

narrative_blocks.title: The Elizabethan Protestant Identity (1558–1603)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.2] Elizabeth I anchored national unity through pragmatic statecraft. Her 1559 Elizabethan Religious Settlement provided a compromise for both sides, creating a Protestant national church with moderate ceremonies that allowed broad outward conformity without religious inquisitions.

She enforced order through modest fines for missing church on Sundays to penalize recusants. When Spain invaded in 1588, England was united by Armada victory, forging a lasting patriotic myth that God favoured Protestant England and strengthening parliamentary support for the Crown.

source.caption: Monumental royal portrait (Woburn Abbey / Queen’s House, Greenwich) showing Elizabeth resting her hand upon the global sphere with the destroyed Spanish Armada in the background.
source.author: George Gower
source.question: How does the Armada Portrait symbolize the transformation of England into an independent, global Protestant maritime power?
source.model_answer: Elizabeth rests her hand directly over the Americas on the globe, flanked by windows showing the stormy destruction of the Catholic Armada on one side and peaceful English ships on the other. It projects that under the Protestant Crown, England had defeated European Catholic hegemony and stood destined for global empire.
source.context: Commissioned following the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588, the portrait forged an indissoluble bond between English national identity and Protestantism.

narrative_blocks.title: The Stuart Rupture: Divine Right (1603–1640)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] The Stuart accession shattered Tudor harmony. James I and Charles I embraced absolutism, insisting through Divine Right that kings claim only God rules them, free from parliamentary consent. Charles ruled eleven years without MPs, extracting illegal taxes without votes through Ship Money.

This tyranny collapsed when Scots rebel against English rules and prayer books. Bankrupted by military resistance, Charles was forced to recall MPs in 1640, triggering an ideological showdown between absolute royal power and parliamentary privilege.

source.title: Source C (Stuart Absolutism): King James I, Speech to Parliament on the Divine Right of Kings (21 March 1610)
source.caption: Address to both Houses of Parliament by James I asserting that kings are God’s lieutenants upon earth and hold absolute authority over statute law and taxation.
source.author: King James I of England (James VI of Scotland)
source.content: The state of monarchy is the supremest thing upon earth; for kings are not only God’s lieutenants upon earth, and sit upon God’s throne, but even by God himself they are called gods... As to dispute what God may do is blasphemy... so is it sedition in subjects to dispute what a king may do in the height of his power.
source.question_badge: SYNOPTIC THEME: STUART DIVINE RIGHT FRICTION
source.question: Why did James I's ideological stance on the Divine Right of Kings alienate an increasingly assertive Parliament?
source.model_answer: James explicitly claimed that kings possessed absolute power above the law and that questioning royal actions was seditious blasphemy. This directly collided with English common law traditions and the House of Commons' belief that their parliamentary liberties and tax approvals were ancient constitutional rights.
source.context: The accession of the Scottish Stuart dynasty in 1603 imported absolutist political theories that caused escalating constitutional conflict with Parliament.

narrative_blocks.title: The Shock of Regicide & Republic (1642–1649)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.4] The Civil War transformed English constitutional history. Parliament's citizen army beat the King at Naseby, ending royal hopes of military victory. Following Charles’s repeated intrigues, Pride's Purge cleared dissenters from Parliament, abolishing the House of Lords and monarchy to establish a republican Commonwealth.

Beheading Charles I in 1649 set a revolutionary precedent: an anointed monarch was held to the law. A ruler who broke his constitutional trust with the people could be tried and executed for treason.

source.title: Source D (Political Philosophy & Statecraft): Frontispiece of Thomas Hobbes’ Leviathan (Abraham Bosse, 1651)
source.caption: Etching by Abraham Bosse for Thomas Hobbes (British Library): A giant sovereign composed of hundreds of individual citizens rising above the landscape, holding sword and crosier.
source.author: Abraham Bosse and Thomas Hobbes
source.question_badge: SYNOPTIC THEME: SOCIAL CONTRACT & CIVIL CHAOS
source.question: How does the frontispiece of Leviathan reflect the traumatic impact of the English Civil War on seventeenth-century political thought?
source.model_answer: Writing in the immediate aftermath of regicide and civil war, Hobbes argued that without an absolute sovereign authority, human life descends into a state of nature that is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. The image shows citizens willingly merging into one Commonwealth to preserve peace and escape civil slaughter.
source.context: Published in 1651 during the Cromwellian Commonwealth, Leviathan founded modern political philosophy by arguing that government authority rests on a social contract to prevent anarchy.

narrative_blocks.title: The 1689 Bill of Rights: Parliamentary Supremacy (1689)
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] The 1688 Glorious Revolution and 1689 Bill of Rights established permanent constitutional monarchy across the realm. Parliament drafted a binding statutory contract with new rulers William III and Mary II, legally ending centuries of royal claims to absolute divine power.

The statute confirmed that the King cannot cancel laws without Parliament, prohibited royal taxes without MP votes, and removed the Crown's royal veto over parliamentary statutes. Sovereignty had shifted decisively from the personal will of the monarch to the supreme authority of the King-in-Parliament.

source.title: Source E (Parliamentary Conditionality): Presentation of the Declaration of Rights to William and Mary (13 February 1689)
source.caption: Contemporary engraving (British Museum) showing the Speaker of the House of Commons presenting the Declaration of Rights to William III and Mary II in the Banqueting House at Whitehall.
source.author: Contemporary London Printmaker
source.question: How does the ceremony depicted in Source E symbolize the ultimate outcome of the 1517–1689 struggle for power in England?
source.model_answer: In the very Banqueting House where Charles I was stepped out to his execution in 1649, William and Mary were offered the English crown only on strict condition that they accept Parliament's Declaration of Rights. Monarchy was transformed from divine right to a contract revocable by Parliament.
source.context: On 13 February 1689, the Convention Parliament formally offered the joint crown to William of Orange and Mary Stuart on condition of upholding parliamentary supremacy.

Every subsequent monarch could reshape church law, turning succession into a life-or-death ideological battleground between Catholics, Anglicans, and Puritans.

sources.caption: Address to both Houses of Parliament by James I asserting that kings are God’s lieutenants upon earth and hold absolute authority over statute law and taxation.

sources.content: The state of monarchy is the supremest thing upon earth; for kings are not only God’s lieutenants upon earth, and sit upon God’s throne, but even by God himself they are called gods... sources.question: Why did James I's ideological stance on the Divine Right of Kings alienate an increasingly assertive Parliament?

tasks.title: Evaluative Historical Essay • Balanced Judgement (3 Paragraphs • 15 mins)
tasks.question: ‘The execution of Charles I in 1649 was the most significant turning point in the struggle between Crown and Parliament.’ How far do you agree?
tasks.prompt: Weigh whether the radical trial and execution of Charles I (1649) or the permanent statutory settlement of the Bill of Rights (1689) was the more decisive turning point in the struggle between Crown and Parliament.

structure_strip: Paragraph 1 (Regicide & Abolition): Analyse how judicial regicide shattered the sacrosanct status of Divine Right and temporarily abolished monarchical governance [5.4].
Paragraph 2 (Statutory Settlement): Evaluate how permanent statutory limits bound the Crown to legal governance, parliamentary consent, and financial oversight in 1689 [5.5].
Conclusion: Reach a weighed comparative verdict: weigh whether physical overthrow and republican experiments represented a more profound transformation than permanent statutory compromise [5.1–5.5].
sentence_starters: Overall, the strongest judgement is that...
On the one hand, a key factor was...
On the other hand, an alternative perspective is that...
In conclusion, the decisive turning point was... because...

hints: Thesis / Argument: State your overall evaluation: agree that 1649 broke the mystical barrier of Divine Right, but argue that 1689 established the permanent legal settlement.
Evidence for 1649 (Regicide): Detail how the High Court of Justice tried Charles I for tyranny and treason, beheading him on 30 January 1649 and abolishing the monarchy.
Evidence for 1689 (Bill of Rights): Detail how William and Mary accepted statutory limits on taxes, armies, and law suspension, making annual Parliaments legally indispensable.
Comparative Conclusion: Synthesize why 1649 was a temporary military upheaval followed by the 1660 Restoration, whereas 1689 was the permanent constitutional victory.
tasks.model_answer:
On the one hand, the public execution of King Charles I in January 1649 was an unprecedented revolutionary turning point. By putting an anointed monarch on trial for high treason against his own people, Parliament irreversibly shattered the Divine Right of Kings. The regicide abolished both the monarchy and the House of Lords, creating England’s first and only republic (the Commonwealth under Oliver Cromwell), demonstrating that a king was legally accountable to the law and to the nation.

On the other hand, the constitutional impact of 1649 proved fragile and short-lived compared to the lasting settlement of 1688–1689. Following Cromwell’s military dictatorship, the Commonwealth collapsed, resulting in the 1660 Restoration where Charles II and James II attempted to reassert absolute royal prerogative. In contrast, the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the 1689 Bill of Rights permanently established constitutional monarchy and parliamentary supremacy. The Crown agreed never to suspend laws, maintain an army, or levy taxes without parliamentary consent, creating a permanent constitutional framework that endures to this day. Therefore, while 1649 was the most radical ideological shock, 1688 was the more enduring and successful turning point.

vocab.definition: The supreme, independent authority and power of a governing body to make laws and govern a state.
Written laws formally passed by Parliament and approved by the monarch, superior to royal decrees.
Compliance with established rules and laws, particularly attending national Church services.
A political system in which a monarch holds total, unrestricted power over government and subjects.
The republican government of England, Scotland, and Ireland established after the execution of Charles I (1649–1660).
An earlier event, legal action, or decision that is regarded as an authoritative guide for future cases.
A system of governance in which a monarch shares power with an elected parliament and rules strictly under the law.
The constitutional right to reject a proposed law or decision made by a law-making body.

video.teacher_guidance: Andrew Chater traces the constitutional culmination of the 17th century: how James II's pro-Catholic policies provoked Parliament to invite William of Orange, cementing the 1689 Bill of Rights. video.viewing_task:
1. [01:15] Recall: Why did the birth of a healthy son to Catholic King James II in June 1688 prompt English politicians to send a secret invitation to William of Orange?
  2. [03:20] Explain: Explain why the overthrow of James II in 1688 was branded the "Glorious Revolution", and why this title is contested by Irish and Scottish historians.
  3. [04:50] Challenge: Synoptic Synthesis: Across the 170-year struggle from Henry VIII (1517) to William and Mary (1689), how did supreme political power shift from Crown to Church to Parliament?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: Protestant MPs had tolerated James II believing his Protestant daughter Mary would succeed him; the birth of a prince guaranteed a permanent Catholic dynasty.
  2. Explain: English Whigs branded it "Glorious" because the transfer of power in London occurred without widespread bloodshed or civil war. However, in Ireland and Scotland, the revolution provoked brutal, bloody warfare (the Battle of the Boyne, the Siege of Derry, and Glencoe), establishing centuries of sectarian oppression.
  3. Challenge: Henry VIII broke with Rome to centralize supreme religious and political power into the absolute royal monarchy. However, royal claims to Divine Right under the Stuarts provoked the Civil War and the execution of Charles I. By 1689, Parliament successfully established that the monarch was a constitutional servant bound by law, making elected Parliament the supreme governing power in Britain.

video.viewing_task:
1. [01:10] Recall: Why did leading English nobles and bishops invite William of Orange and Mary to intervene against King James II in 1688?
  2. [03:20] Explain: Explain two legal limits placed permanently on royal power by the 1689 Bill of Rights.
  3. [05:30] Challenge: Looking across 1517–1689 (Henry VIII's Royal Supremacy, 1649 Regicide, and 1689 Bill of Rights), who ultimately won the struggle between Crown, Church, and Parliament?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: James II suspended Parliamentary laws, promoted Catholics to high office, and the birth of a Catholic male heir in June 1688 threatened a permanent Catholic dynasty.
  2. Explain: Monarchs could no longer suspend laws, levy taxes without Parliamentary grant, or maintain a peacetime standing army without Parliament's consent, while regular free elections and parliamentary free speech were guaranteed.
  3. Challenge: Whereas Henry VIII concentrated supreme spiritual and political power in the Crown in 1534, by 1689 Parliament emerged decisively sovereign—creating a constitutional monarchy where kings ruled only through Parliamentary statute.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Between 1517 and 1689, supreme [Sovereignty] in England shifted decisively away from royal [Absolutism]. key_individuals.name: Martin Luther
key_individuals.role: German Monk, Professor of Theology & Catalyst of the Reformation
key_individuals.origins: German monk and scholar in Wittenberg outraged by friars selling papal indulgences—certificates claiming cash payments could free souls from Purgatory.
key_individuals.significance: Challenged papal authority in October 1517 with his Ninety-Five Theses; rapidly multiplied by printing presses across Europe, his ideas shattered Catholic unity and launched the Protestant Reformation.
achievements: Published his 95 Theses at Wittenberg in October 1517 condemning corrupt indulgence sales.

Translated the Bible into vernacular German and inspired Protestant reformers across Europe (ironically prompting young Henry VIII to write a Catholic defence that won him the papal title "Defender of the Faith").

key_individuals.name: King Henry VIII
key_individuals.role: Tudor King Who Broke with Rome (1509–1547)
key_individuals.origins: Second Tudor monarch desperate by 1527 for a legitimate male heir to secure the Tudor succession and marry Anne Boleyn, yet blocked when Emperor Charles V’s troops held Pope Clement VII captive in Rome.
key_individuals.significance: Used statute laws passed through the Reformation Parliament to sever England from the Pope—declaring himself Supreme Head of the Church of England under the 1534 Act of Supremacy and dissolving over 800 monasteries (1536–40).
achievements: Dismissed Cardinal Wolsey (1529) after the failed Blackfriars legatine court and relied on Thomas Cromwell and Archbishop Thomas Cranmer to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon (1533).
Enacted the 1534 Act of Supremacy and Treasons Act (executing dissenters such as Sir Thomas More) while dissolving 800+ monasteries and selling their lands to English gentry.
Crucially worked through parliamentary statute rather than solo decree, unintentionally strengthening the constitutional authority of King-in-Parliament.

key_individuals.name: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey & Thomas Cromwell
key_individuals.role: Chief Ministers of King Henry VIII Before & During the Break with Rome
key_individuals.origins: Cardinal Wolsey served as Lord Chancellor and papal legate trying to win an annulment through diplomacy with Rome; lawyer Thomas Cromwell succeeded him with a revolutionary parliamentary strategy.
key_individuals.significance: Where Wolsey fell in 1529 because Pope Clement VII (dominated by Emperor Charles V) revoked the London annulment trial, Cromwell engineered England’s statutory Break with Rome (1533–34) and the Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–40).
achievements: Wolsey’s 1529 Blackfriars legatine court collapsed when Pope Clement VII recalled the case to Rome, ending Wolsey’s career.
Cromwell steered the 1533 Act in Restraint of Appeals and 1534 Act of Supremacy through the Reformation Parliament, halted annates taxes to Rome, and surveyed and dissolved 800+ monasteries.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Wolsey worked inside Catholic papal law and failed to secure Henry’s annulment; Cromwell bypassed Rome entirely using sovereign Acts of Parliament.

key_individuals.name: Queen Elizabeth I
key_individuals.role: Tudor Queen & Architect of the 1559 "Middle Way" (1558–1603)
key_individuals.origins: Daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn who inherited a religiously fractured England in November 1558 after Mary I burned nearly 300 Protestant martyrs and exiled Puritans demanded radical Calvinist reform.
key_individuals.significance: Stabilised England via the 1559 Elizabethan Religious Settlement (Via Media / Middle Way), survived Pope Pius V’s 1570 excommunication and Catholic plots centred on Mary, Queen of Scots, and defeated Philip II’s 1588 Spanish Armada.
achievements: Passed the 1559 Act of Supremacy (taking the moderate title "Supreme Governor") and Act of Uniformity (English Book of Common Prayer, Compromise communion wording, and 12d recusancy fines rather than heresy burnings).

Crushed the 1569 Revolt of the Northern Earls, relied on Sir Francis Walsingham’s spy network to foil the 1586 Babington Plot, and reluctantly signed Mary, Queen of Scots’ death warrant (executed February 1587).
Celebrated victory over the 1588 Spanish Armada ("God blew and they were scattered"), cementing England’s Protestant and naval identity.

key_individuals.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
key_individuals.role: Catholic Claimant to the English Throne
key_individuals.origins: Catholic cousin of Elizabeth I who fled Scotland into English captivity in 1568 and immediately became the figurehead for Catholic plots to depose Elizabeth, especially after Pope Pius V’s 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis.
key_individuals.significance: Caught endorsing Anthony Babington’s 1586 assassination plot in coded letters smuggled inside beer barrels and decrypted by Walsingham’s codebreakers, leading to her execution at Fotheringhay Castle in February 1587—and giving Philip II his final pretext to launch the Armada.
achievements: Focal point of the 1569 Northern Earls’ Rebellion and successive foreign-backed Catholic conspiracies.
Convicted of treason in 1586 after Sir Francis Walsingham intercepted and decoded her Babington Plot correspondence; beheaded in February 1587.

key_individuals.name: Sir Francis Walsingham
key_individuals.role: Principal Secretary & Protestant Spymaster to Queen Elizabeth I
key_individuals.origins: Devout Protestant statesman who built an intelligence network of double agents, overseas informers, and cryptographers across Europe to protect Elizabeth I after her 1570 papal excommunication.
key_individuals.significance: Uncovered Catholic assassination conspiracies culminating in the 1586 Babington Plot—intercepting letters hidden in beer-barrel bungs and breaking Mary Stuart’s cipher to secure the hard proof Parliament needed for Mary’s execution.
achievements: Operated an international espionage and codebreaking service protecting Elizabeth I from post-1570 assassination plots.
Trapped Anthony Babington and Mary, Queen of Scots in 1586 by decrypting their beer-barrel correspondence.

key_individuals.name: King Philip II of Spain
key_individuals.role: Catholic Ruler of the Spanish Empire & Architect of the 1588 Armada
key_individuals.origins: Devout Catholic Habsburg monarch provoked by English military support for Protestant Dutch rebels, Sir Francis Drake’s privateering raids on Spanish treasure, and the February 1587 execution of Mary, Queen of Scots.
key_individuals.significance: Launched the 130-ship Spanish Armada under the Duke of Medina Sidonia in July 1588 to ferry the Duke of Parma’s Flanders army across the Channel and overthrow Protestant England—ending in catastrophic defeat off Calais, Gravelines, and stormy Scottish and Irish coasts.
achievements: Assembled the 130-ship Armada (delayed a year by Drake’s April 1587 Cadiz raid) sailing in tight defensive crescent formation.

Lost half his fleet after English fireships scattered the Calais anchorage (7–8 August 1588), culverin broadsides battered Spanish galleons at Gravelines, and Atlantic gales wrecked dozens of ships off Scotland and Ireland.

key_individuals.name: Sir Francis Drake
key_individuals.role: Elizabethan Privateer, Circumnavigator & Vice-Admiral Against the Armada
key_individuals.origins: Audacious English sea captain and privateer whose raids on Spanish Caribbean ports and treasure fleets infuriated King Philip II.
key_individuals.significance: Delayed the Spanish Armada for a crucial year by raiding Cadiz in April 1587 ("singeing the King of Spain’s beard") and served alongside Lord Howard in 1588 using fast race-built galleons, long-range culverin broadsides, and Calais fireships.
achievements: Raided Cadiz harbour in April 1587, destroying ~30 ships and burning seasoned barrel staves—forcing Spain to store Armada food and water in green wood that rotted at sea.
Helped shatter the scattered Spanish crescent formation at the Battle of Gravelines (August 1588).

key_individuals.name: King James I & King Charles I
key_individuals.role: Stuart Monarchs Who Championed the Divine Right of Kings
key_individuals.origins: Scottish Stuart monarchs (from 1603) who embraced absolutism and the Divine Right of Kings—insisting monarchs answered to God alone rather than to elected Members of Parliament.
key_individuals.significance: Charles I ruled for eleven years without Parliament (1629–40, taxing inland counties via Ship Money defied by John Hampden in 1637), backed Archbishop William Laud’s unpopular High Church reforms, raided the Commons to arrest Five MPs (January 1642), lost the Civil War, and was tried and beheaded for high treason on 30 January 1649.
achievements: James I articulated Divine Right theory; Charles I dismissed Parliament in 1629 for the "Eleven Years’ Tyranny" (Personal Rule) funded by inland Ship Money.
Recalled Parliament in 1640 after Scots rebelled against Laud’s prayer book, marched armed guards into the Commons on 4 January 1642, and raised his royal standard at Nottingham in August 1642.
Defeated at Naseby (1645), sparked a Second Civil War, and following Pride’s Purge was tried and executed outside Whitehall on 30 January 1649—proving even an anointed king stood beneath the law.

key_individuals.name: Archbishop William Laud
key_individuals.role: Archbishop of Canterbury Under King Charles I (1633–1645)
key_individuals.origins: Charles I’s chief religious minister during the Personal Rule, who enforced ceremonial "beauty of holiness" reforms (railed altars, vestments) that Puritans feared were a secret return to Catholicism.
key_individuals.significance: Persecuted Puritan critics and attempted to impose a new English-style prayer book on Presbyterian Scotland—triggering the Scottish rebellion that bankrupted Charles I and forced him to recall Parliament in 1640.
achievements: Enforced High Church ceremonial uniformity across English parishes during the 1630s.
Triggered Scottish armed resistance, leading the recalled Long Parliament to impeach and imprison Laud.

key_individuals.name: Oliver Cromwell & The New Model Army
key_individuals.role: Parliamentary Cavalry Commander & Lord Protector of the Commonwealth (1653–1658)
key_individuals.origins: Puritan East Anglian MP who helped create Parliament’s professional, merit-promoted New Model Army in 1645 alongside Sir Thomas Fairfax.
key_individuals.significance: Routed Charles I’s Royalists with disciplined cavalry charges at the Battle of Naseby (June 1645), signed Charles I’s 1649 death warrant after Pride’s Purge, and ruled republican Britain as Lord Protector of the Commonwealth (1653–58).
achievements: Built the full-time, red-coated New Model Army (1645), where officers were promoted on merit rather than aristocratic birth, winning the decisive Battle of Naseby (14 June 1645).
Backed the January 1649 trial and execution of Charles I ("man of blood"), abolishing the monarchy and House of Lords to establish the Commonwealth.

key_individuals.name: William III & Mary II (1689 Bill of Rights)
key_individuals.role: Joint Constitutional Monarchs Bound by the 1689 Bill of Rights
key_individuals.origins: After the 1660 Restoration, Catholic King James II’s clashes with Parliament led Protestant nobles in 1688 to invite his Protestant daughter Mary and her husband, Dutch Prince William of Orange, to intervene.
key_individuals.significance: Landed at Torbay in November 1688 as James II fled to France ("Glorious Revolution") and accepted the Crown under the binding December 1689 Bill of Rights—permanently ending royal absolutism and establishing constitutional monarchy under King-in-Parliament.
achievements: Accepted Parliament’s Declaration of Rights (February 1689), enacted into statute as the Bill of Rights (December 1689).
Confirmed by law that monarchs could never again suspend parliamentary statutes or levy taxes without MPs’ consent.

guided_reading.book_title: Letters on the Dissolution of the Monasteries & Robert Aske’s Pilgrimage Oath (1536)
guided_reading.author: Royal Commissioners & Robert Aske (1536 • The National Archives SP 1)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Hans Holbein the Younger, Portrait of Thomas Cromwell (c. 1532–1533), King Henry VIII’s Chief Minister who masterminded the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
guided_reading.author_context: After breaking with Rome under the 1534 Act of Supremacy, King Henry VIII and his Chief Minister Thomas Cromwell compiled the Valor Ecclesiasticus tax survey (1535) and sent royal commissioners to inspect and close over 800 monasteries across England, Wales, and Ireland. In October 1536, Yorkshire lawyer Robert Aske led 30,000 northern rebels in the "Pilgrimage of Grace" to defend their parish faith and local abbeys.
guided_reading.extract:
From the Report of Cromwell’s Royal Commissioners on suppressing northern religious houses (1536): "According to the King’s Highness’s commission, we have taken the surrender of the lesser abbeys, stripped the lead from the roofs for the royal treasury, weighed the silver chalices and jeweled shrines, and discharged the monks. Their lands and annual rents shall henceforth augment the revenues of the Crown."

From Robert Aske’s Proclamation and Testimony on why Yorkshire rose in the Pilgrimage of Grace (October 1536): "In the northern parts the abbeys gave great alms to poor men, sheltered travellers across the wild moors where no inns stand, lent seed-corn to tenants in hard seasons, and maintained sea-walls, bridges, and highways. Now the ornaments of God’s churches are carted away, their stone walls pulled down, and poor folk left without succour at the abbey gate.

Therefore we take our Pilgrim’s Oath beneath the Banner of the Five Wounds of Christ—not as traitors against our Sovereign Lord the King, but to petition His Grace to expel base-born evil counsellors such as Cromwell and restore the ancient liberties of Holy Church."

vocabVault.def: Henry VIII and Thomas Cromwell’s closure and seizure of more than 800 monasteries, priories, and convents between 1536 and 1540.
Charitable food, money, and shelter given to the poor and sick—a major community role of medieval monasteries.
The massive 1536 northern Tudor uprising of around 30,000 people led by Robert Aske against monastery closures and religious change.
Henry VIII’s 1534 legal claim to be Supreme Head of the Church of England in place of the Pope.

parent_discussion.question: Looking at the Royal Commissioners’ report, was Henry VIII closing monasteries only for religious reform, or also for wealth?
parent_discussion.answer: Stripping roof lead, melting silver shrines, and seizing monastic rents doubled royal income and paid for coastal forts and wars.

parent_discussion.question: Why did ordinary northern families in Yorkshire care so deeply when their local abbeys were shut down?
parent_discussion.answer: Beyond religion, monasteries provided charity (alms) for the poor, safe lodging for travellers, loans for farmers, and upkeep of roads and bridges.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Robert Aske carefully blame "evil counsellors such as Cromwell" rather than attacking Henry VIII directly?
parent_discussion.answer: Openly rebelling against an anointed Tudor monarch was high treason, so Tudor rebels traditionally claimed to be loyal subjects rescuing the King from bad advisers.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: What happened to the roof lead, silver plate, and lands of England’s 800 monasteries?

Pair: Compare the motives of Cromwell’s commissioners with Robert Aske’s defence of northern abbeys.

Share: Was Henry VIII’s Reformation driven mainly by religion, dynastic marriage, or money?
questions: Which Chief Minister organised the inspection and closure of England’s monasteries?
List three practical services Robert Aske says northern abbeys provided to local communities.
What banner did the rebels carry during the October 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Condensed and modernised in spelling from 1536 Tudor State Papers (TNA SP 1) and Robert Aske’s Pilgrimage of Grace oath.

guided_reading.book_title: The Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559) & "Windows into Men’s Souls"
guided_reading.author: Act of Uniformity (1559) & Sir Francis Bacon ("Observations", 1592)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Robert Peake the Elder, Procession Portrait of Queen Elizabeth I (c. 1600–1601), depicting the Protestant monarch carried in state surrounded by her courtiers.
guided_reading.author_context: When twenty-five-year-old Elizabeth I inherited the throne in November 1558 after the turbulent reigns of Edward VI (strictly Protestant) and Mary I (strictly Catholic), Europe was tearing itself apart in wars of religion. Through her 1559 Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity, Elizabeth crafted a pragmatic "Middle Way" (Via Media), later famously summarised by statesman Sir Francis Bacon.
guided_reading.extract:
From Queen Elizabeth I’s Act of Uniformity (1559): "Every person inhabiting within this realm, having no lawful or reasonable excuse to be absent, shall diligently and faithfully resort to their parish church upon every Sunday and other holy days, and then and there abide orderly and soberly during the time of Common Prayer in English... upon pain of punishment by the censures of the Church, and also upon pain that every person so offending shall forfeit for every such offence twelve pence, to be levied by the churchwardens for the use of the poor of the same parish."

From Sir Francis Bacon’s contemporary reflection on Queen Elizabeth’s statecraft (1592): "Her Majesty, not liking to make windows into men’s hearts and secret thoughts—except the abundance of them did overflow into overt and express acts of sedition or treasonous disobedience against the State—tempered the severity of the laws, requiring outward conformity in the parish church while sparing tender consciences from the fires that had burned in the reign before."

vocabVault.def: Elizabeth I’s 1559 religious compromise blending Protestant English services with traditional church ornaments and bishops.
A Catholic who refused to attend Protestant Church of England Sunday services and paid fines instead.
Obeying the law in public by attending Sunday church, without the government interrogating private beliefs.
The careful title Elizabeth I chose in 1559 (instead of Henry VIII’s "Supreme Head") to reduce offence to Catholics and Puritans.

parent_discussion.question: What was the fine in 1559 for missing Sunday service at your parish church without a good excuse, and where did the money go?
parent_discussion.answer: Twelve pence (one shilling—several days’ wages for a labourer!), collected by churchwardens to support the poor of the parish.

parent_discussion.question: What did Sir Francis Bacon mean by saying Elizabeth did not want to "make windows into men’s hearts and secret thoughts"?
parent_discussion.answer: Unlike Mary I who burned heretics for private beliefs, Elizabeth cared mainly about outward loyalty and peace, leaving private thoughts alone unless someone plotted treason.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Elizabeth’s tolerant Middle Way grow much harsher toward Catholics after 1570?
parent_discussion.answer: In 1570 Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth (Regnans in Excelsis) and urged Catholics to overthrow her, sparking plots around Mary, Queen of Scots, and Spain.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: In what language were Church of England services held under the 1559 Settlement?

Pair: Why did Elizabeth choose the title "Supreme Governor" rather than "Supreme Head"?

Share: Did Elizabeth’s Middle Way satisfy everyone, or was it a clever political truce that kept England out of civil war?
questions: How much did an absent parishioner have to pay under the 1559 Act of Uniformity?
Who collected those fines, and whom was the money used to help?
Quote the famous metaphor Sir Francis Bacon used to describe Elizabeth’s attitude toward private religious belief.
guided_reading.provenance_note: Combines modernised wording from the 1559 Act of Uniformity with Sir Francis Bacon’s 1592 commentary on Elizabeth I.

guided_reading.book_title: Queen Elizabeth I’s Speech to the Troops at Tilbury Camp (9 August 1588)
guided_reading.author: Queen Elizabeth I (preserved by Dr Leonel Sharp • British Library Harley MS 6798)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Sixteenth-century engraving of the 38-gun English flagship Ark Royal, commanded by Lord Howard of Effingham against the Spanish Armada in 1588.
guided_reading.author_context: In August 1588, even after English fireships scattered King Philip II’s 130-ship Spanish Armada off Calais and Gravelines, England feared that the Duke of Parma’s veteran Spanish army in Flanders might still land along the Thames estuary. Riding on a white horse in a polished breastplate at Tilbury Camp in Essex on 9 August 1588, Elizabeth I delivered one of the most famous speeches in English history, recorded by chaplain Dr Leonel Sharp.
guided_reading.extract:
"My loving people, we have been persuaded by some that are careful of our safety, to take heed how we commit ourselves to armed multitudes, for fear of treachery; but I assure you I do not desire to live to distrust my faithful and loving people. Let tyrants fear! I have always so behaved myself that, under God, I have placed my chiefest strength and safeguard in the loyal hearts and good-will of my subjects.

And therefore I am come amongst you, as you see, at this time, not for my recreation and disport, but being resolved, in the midst and heat of the battle, to live and die amongst you all; to lay down for my God, and for my kingdom, and for my people, my honour and my blood, even in the dust.

I know I have the body but of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm; to which, rather than any dishonour shall grow by me, I myself will take up arms, I myself will be your general, judge, and rewarder of every one of your virtues in the field."

vocabVault.def: The great fleet of 130 Spanish warships sent by King Philip II in 1588 to escort an invasion army from Flanders to England.
Eight old ships packed with pitch, gunpowder, and tar set ablaze at midnight off Calais to break the Spanish crescent formation.
Commander of the powerful Spanish army waiting in the Spanish Netherlands (Flanders) to cross the Channel.
The art of persuasive public speaking used by leaders to inspire loyalty and courage.

parent_discussion.question: Why had Elizabeth’s cautious advisers warned her against riding out into the middle of thousands of armed soldiers at Tilbury?
parent_discussion.answer: They feared an assassin or Catholic sympathiser in the crowd might try to kill the unmarried Protestant Queen.

parent_discussion.question: How does Elizabeth turn sixteenth-century prejudices about female rulers upside down in her most famous sentence?
parent_discussion.answer: She acknowledges male expectations ("the body of a weak and feeble woman") only to declare she possesses "the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too."

parent_discussion.question: Was the Spanish Armada defeated mainly by speeches and storms ("God blew"), or by English naval design and tactics?
parent_discussion.answer: While Tilbury boosted morale and Atlantic gales wrecked fleeing ships, nimble race-built galleons like Ark Royal, long-range culverin guns, and Calais fireships broke the Spanish plan first.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Where in England is Tilbury, and why were English troops camped there in August 1588?

Pair: Pick out two phrases Elizabeth uses to contrast herself with foreign "tyrants."

Share: How did defeating the Armada shape Tudor Protestant propaganda?
questions: Where does Elizabeth say she places her "chiefest strength and safeguard"?
Quote the famous line in which Elizabeth contrasts her physical body with her royal courage.
Which foreign commander and country does Elizabeth name with "foul scorn"?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original text of Queen Elizabeth I’s 1588 Tilbury speech as preserved by chaplain Dr Leonel Sharp (BL Harley MS 6798).

guided_reading.book_title: The Trial & Scaffold Speech of King Charles I (January 1649)
guided_reading.author: Westminster Hall High Court Record & King Charles I (20–30 January 1649)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Studio of Sir Anthony van Dyck, Portrait of King Charles I in Garter Robes (c. 1636), embodying the Stuart ideal of Divine Right majesty.
guided_reading.author_context: After seven years of bitter Civil War between Royalists ("Cavaliers") and Parliamentarians ("Roundheads") and Oliver Cromwell’s New Model Army, Parliament put an anointed monarch on public trial for treason in Westminster Hall in January 1649. This verbatim clash between Lord President John Bradshaw and King Charles I crystallised two irreconcilable visions of power: Divine Right monarchy versus accountability to the people.
guided_reading.extract:
In Westminster Hall on 20 January 1649, King Charles I refused even to remove his hat or enter a plea before the sixty-eight Parliamentary Commissioners: "I would know by what power I am called hither... Remember, I am your King, your lawful King, and what sins you bring upon your heads, and the judgment of God upon this land. Think well upon it, before you go further from one sin to a greater. A King cannot be tried by any superior jurisdiction on earth!"

Lord President John Bradshaw replied sternly on behalf of the Commons of England: "Sir, you have held yourself accountable to none save God alone; yet there is a contract and a bargain made between the King and his people, and your oath is taken for the performance of it. The bond is reciprocal: as you are their liege lord, so are you bound to govern according to the laws of the land, and not otherwise!"

Ten days later, standing on the frost-covered scaffold outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649, Charles I addressed his final words before the axe fell: "For the people, truly I desire their liberty and freedom as much as anybody whomsoever; but I must tell you that their liberty and freedom consists in having of government, not for having a share in government: a subject and a sovereign are clean different things."

vocabVault.def: The Stuart belief that monarchs were appointed directly by God and could not be judged or removed by any earthly Parliament.
The deliberate trial and execution (killing) of a reigning monarch.
The republican government without a king or House of Lords established in England after Charles I’s execution in 1649.
A supreme ruler—such as a king or queen—contrasted by Charles I with ordinary "subjects".

parent_discussion.question: Why did King Charles I refuse to take off his hat or plead "guilty" or "not guilty" in Westminster Hall?
parent_discussion.answer: Entering a plea would recognise Parliament’s court as legal; Charles believed by Divine Right that no earthly court had authority to judge an anointed king.

parent_discussion.question: How did Judge John Bradshaw argue that a king CAN commit treason against his own country?
parent_discussion.answer: Bradshaw argued kingship is a two-way contract: the people owe loyalty only so long as the king governs within the laws of England rather than waging war on his subjects.

parent_discussion.question: What did Charles I mean on the scaffold by saying "a subject and a sovereign are clean different things"?
parent_discussion.answer: Right up to his death, he believed ordinary people had a right to fair laws, but zero right to vote on or share political power.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why had Charles I clashed so bitterly with Parliament between 1629 (Ship Money / Eleven Years’ Tyranny) and 1642?

Pair: Whose argument in Westminster Hall sounds more convincing to a modern citizen—and whose would have shocked most 17th-century Europeans?

Share: Why did England bring back the monarchy in 1660, yet permanently limit royal power in the 1689 Bill of Rights?
questions: Where in London was King Charles I put on trial in January 1649?
What "reciprocal" agreement did Lord President Bradshaw say existed between a king and his people?
On what date was Charles I executed outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original exchanges from the January 1649 Westminster Hall trial record and King Charles I’s scaffold speech, framed with brief context.

guided_reading.book_title: Two Treatises of Government & The Bill of Rights (1689)
guided_reading.author: John Locke (1689) & Parliamentary Bill of Rights (1 Will. & Mar. Sess. 2 c. 2)
guided_reading.cover_caption: Historical painting depicting Parliament presenting the Declaration of Rights to William III and Mary II in Whitehall on 13 February 1689.
guided_reading.author_context: After Catholic King James II tried to suspend Parliament’s laws and rule without consent, Parliament invited Protestant William of Orange and Mary Stuart to take the throne in the "Glorious Revolution" of 1688–1689—strictly on condition that they accepted the Bill of Rights. English philosopher John Locke published Two Treatises of Government in 1689 to explain why legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed.
guided_reading.extract:
From the Parliamentary Bill of Rights (December 1689), ending absolute monarchy in Britain: "The Lords Spiritual and Temporal and Commons, assembled at Westminster, declare:
1. That the pretended power of suspending of laws or the execution of laws by regal authority without consent of Parliament is illegal.
4. That levying money for or to the use of the Crown by pretence of prerogative, without grant of Parliament, is illegal.
6. That the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, unless it be with consent of Parliament, is against law.
9. That the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament."

From John Locke’s Second Treatise of Government (1689): "Men being by nature all free, equal, and independent, no one can be subjected to the political power of another without his own consent. Whenever the legislators or prince endeavour to take away and destroy the property and liberties of the people, or to reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people, who are thereupon absolved from any further obedience."

vocabVault.def: A system in which a king or queen reigns as head of state, but real law-making and taxing power belongs to an elected Parliament.
Personal royal powers once used by Tudor and Stuart monarchs to bypass Parliament.
A permanent full-time professional army kept during peacetime, which Parliament forbade without its approval.
John Locke’s principle that rulers only hold rightful authority if the people agree to how they are governed.

parent_discussion.question: Look across the whole Tudor and Stuart story (1517–1689): who held supreme power under Henry VIII in 1534 compared with William and Mary in 1689?
parent_discussion.answer: In 1534 the Crown dominated both Church and Parliament; by 1689 Parliament had won supreme authority over laws, taxes, the army, and even who wore the crown.

parent_discussion.question: Which specific abuses of King Charles I and King James II were banned forever by Clauses 1, 4, 6, and 9 of the 1689 Bill of Rights?
parent_discussion.answer: Ignoring Parliament’s laws, collecting unapproved taxes (like Ship Money), keeping a peacetime army to intimidate citizens, and arresting MPs for speaking freely in Parliament.

parent_discussion.question: How did John Locke’s 1689 ideas later influence revolutions far beyond Britain?
parent_discussion.answer: His argument that people are "free, equal, and independent" and may replace rulers who abuse power directly inspired the 1776 American Declaration of Independence and modern democracies.

guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Why was 1688–1689 called the "Glorious" or "Bloodless" Revolution in England?

Pair: Match Clauses 1, 4, 6, and 9 of the Bill of Rights to earlier Stuart clashes you studied in Enquiry 4.

Share: By 1689, who had won the 170-year struggle between Crown, Church, and Parliament?
questions: According to the 1689 Bill of Rights, whose consent is required to levy taxes or keep a peacetime standing army?
Where does Clause 9 guarantee complete freedom of speech and debate?
According to John Locke, what makes political power over free people legitimate?
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original clauses from the 1689 Parliamentary Bill of Rights paired with John Locke’s Two Treatises of Government (1689).
